zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check only, after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima, with Taichi Aida; source licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). Transcription choices and English review notes here are this reviewer's scan-based work, not a reproduction of the headword dataset.

lines.note: Jisei is a deathbed verse or saying; yoqi cotoba means good words. The scan supports cotoba, not OCR coroba; consonantal initial I makes Iixei jisei, not iisei.
Completes the definition: words spoken when one is about to die. Preserve the printed pera and the short s in estando rather than modernizing the wording.
Jisetsu denotes the time or occasion. The example begins jisetsu toorai, the arrival of the time; final t in Iixet is the historical checked-coda notation.

runs.text: Chegarſe, ou vir a hora, ou tempo.

lines.note: Suru completes the example about the time arriving. The Portuguese explicitly gives both hora and tempo, confirming the temporal meaning.

Jishi is one's own excrement, identified by waga fun. The scan reads lowercase fun rather than OCR Fuu; the odd-looking Portuguese ſuidade is retained as printed, and eſter continues below without a securely visible terminal hyphen.
Co completes eſterco. Jishi kusaki koto wo shirazu says that one does not perceive one's own excrement as foul; Xix. is the source label, not part of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Ninguem ſe conhece aſi meſmo. Aßi como lhe

lines.note: The Portuguese interprets the saying as failure to recognize one's own faults, then compares this with not smelling one's own excrement. The visible separation in aſi meſmo is retained.
Completes the comparison: one's own excrement does not smell bad to oneself. The source's esterco and historical typography are preserved.
This homophonous jishi entry means two children, explicitly explained by futari no ko and dous filhos; it is distinct from the preceding excrement entry.
Here jishi means one's own child, as waga ko and filho proprio show. The separate headword line must not be merged with the preceding homophone.
This jishi denotes a young child, explained by chigo ko and Portuguese minino. The printed i, is an explanatory marker, not an additional Japanese syllable.
Jishin is oneself in person, explained by mizukara no mi. Eu, not OCR Du, supplies the Portuguese first-person pronoun; the scan's doubled z in Mizzucarano is retained.
Jishin te wo kudaku describes personally applying considerable effort. The Portuguese peſ- begins peſſoalmente on the next row; the visible terminal hyphen is retained.
Completes peſſoalmente, specifying that the effort is made in person. This short continuation is its own physical line.
A different jishin means a compassionate heart and is equated with jihishin. Iifixin uses f for the historical h-row sound; neither the headword nor the synonym begins with OCR F or ſ.
Completes miſericordioſo, merciful, the second Portuguese description of the compassionate heart.
This jishin denotes one's own heart, explained by mizukara ga kokoro. Cora- begins coração; it is a new homophonous entry, not a continuation of the compassionate-heart gloss.
Completes coração, then gives jishin wo korasu. The Portuguese interprets it as self-mortification, with the inward qualification on the next line.
Interiormente specifies that the preceding mortification is inward or spiritual. Its connection is to the example, not the next entry.
Jishoo is one's own nature, with mizukara no shoo as the Japanese explanation. Both long-o signs are visibly carons.
Ou natural supplies a second Portuguese expression for one's natural disposition. It completes the preceding definition.
A separate jishoo means praising oneself. The example begins jishoo wo; the source's aßi meſmo is preserved.
Yuu completes jishoo wo yuu, speaking in self-praise. Idem indicates that this example has the already stated meaning.

runs.text: Iixǒ. Tadaxij ji. i, Iino xǒ.

lines.note: This jishoo concerns the form of written characters, explained by tadashii ji and ji no shoo. A small raised terminal mark after for is visible; it begins forma on the next row.
Ma completes forma. Jishoo ga yoi or warui says the character-form is good or bad; l is the printed alternative marker, not Japanese.

runs.text: a forma da letra boa, ou ruim.

lines.note: Completes ser with the two evaluations of the written letter's shape. This is about letter-form, not the truth of its content.
Jishu is the person who keeps time, literally one who watches the hours. Relogeiro is retained as the printed Portuguese word.
Completes the occupational gloss as one responsible for the hours. It clarifies the timekeeper sense rather than requiring the narrower modern sense of clockmaker.

runs.text: Hũa certa ſeita de Iapão, que deſcen-

lines.note: Jishuu names a Japanese religious school. The Portuguese says it descends from the group named on the next line; the visible terminal hyphen divides deſcende.

Completes the descent of the Jishuu sect from the Joodoshuu tradition. The local print is transcribed Iǔdǒxùs: first ǔ, then ǒ, and final ù before s. The vowel forms/marks are irregular and partly weak; this selected reading is not normalized to the expected sect name. The term is embedded in Portuguese.
Jissei here denotes the sun and stars, explicitly hi and hoshi. S. is the upright written-register label, outside the italic gloss.
This separate jissei is the sun's influence or force, hi no ikioi. The final S. again marks written usage and is not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Jissetsu denotes true news or a reliable report. The object-marked Iixxetuo begins an example about establishing its truth by hearing.
Kiki kiwamuru means hearing thoroughly or ascertaining by inquiry. The scan shows Ouuir and a space before bem; ver- begins verdadeiras.
Completes verdadeiras, qualifying the news as true. This row is part of the preceding example, not an independent entry.
Jisshi isshoo describes extreme danger, explained as nine of ten dying. The scan reads osnoue rather than OCR esnoue; the tightly printed article and numeral remain joined.
Completes the contrast with one surviving. The example begins a battle of jisshi isshoo, a fight attended by extreme risk.
Nasu completes the Japanese battle expression. The Portuguese says to fight in great danger; riſ- visibly continues as riſco.

runs.text: co da vida onde os noue morrem, & hum vi-

lines.note: Completes risco da vida and describes nine dying while one lives. The terminal vi- visibly divides viue at the physical line boundary.
Ue completes viue. The new example applies the same extreme-danger expression to illness, with wadzurai wo suru; the draft's tightly joined Iixxiixxǒno is retained.

runs.text: Estar doente de doença perigoſa, de que polla

lines.note: Begins the illness example's translation: to suffer a dangerous disease. Polla is the printed historical form, not silently changed to modern pela.

runs.text: mòr parte morrem os que a tem.

lines.note: Completes the relative clause: most people who have the disease die. The grave in mòr and the unaccented printed tem are retained.
Jisshi is a true or legitimate child, explained by makoto no ko. Filho is clearly supported by the scan, repairing OCR flho; le- starts legitimo.
Completes legitimo, legitimate, the second qualification of the child. The physical continuation remains separate.
Jisshin means daily renewal or progress, with hibi ni arata nari as the explanation. The gloss's crecendo is the visible historical spelling and is not supplied with an extra s.
The growth applies to virtue, learning, and similar accomplishments. Iixxin- begins the illustrative construction across the line break.
Completes jisshin no koo wo hagemasu, applying oneself to daily progress. The scan supports dia rather than OCR di; the Portuguese sentence continues at the top of column 2.
Completes the sentence carried from column 1: making greater progress in learning and virtue. The final upright S. marks written usage; mòr/mòres is retained rather than modernized.
Jisshoo is genuine proof or testimony, explained by makoto no shooko. The headword has two x letters, not OCR lixixô; the visible circumflex contrasts with the following entry's caron.
Completes teſtemunho verdadeiro, true testimony. The physical split belongs inside the Portuguese word.
This jisshoo is something true and right, with makoto and masashii as explanations. The headword's caron is distinct from the circumflex in the preceding proof entry.
Completes the gloss with recta, then illustrates establishing the truth by hearing or inquiry. The extra OCR comma after the italic span is not present in the scan.

runs.text: Ouuir afirmandoſe bẽ ſe he couſa certa.

lines.note: The example means listening while making sure the matter is certain. Bẽ is the printed nasal abbreviation and is not expanded.
Jisshoku here denotes the sun's visible colour, hi no iro. The tightly printed Coraparente is retained rather than reinterpreting the word as the modern eclipse sense.
Jiyaku means temple duties or offices, literally tera no yaku. The initial is I, repairing OCR liyacu.
Varela is the alternative Portuguese designation for the religious establishment. The phrase completes the institutional-duty gloss.

runs.text: Iiyacu. Mizzucarano cuſuri. i, Vaga nomu

lines.note: A separate jiyaku concerns one's own medicine: mizukara no kusuri, or what one oneself drinks or takes. The Japanese explanation continues on the next row.

runs.text: Mezinha que eu tomo por mim.

lines.note: Kusuri completes waga nomu kusuri. The gloss identifies medicine that I take myself; Mezinha, not OCR Mſezinha, is supported by the scan.
Jiyo literally includes self and others, ware and hito. The Portuguese begins to explain a narrower usual sense, with comunmen- continuing below.

runs.text: te no vſo ſe toma pellos outros. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the statement that ordinary usage takes the term to mean the others. Iiyoni begins the following comparison.
Jiyo ni konzenu hito is someone not mixed with or indistinguishable from the others. The Portuguese calls him notable or different; the printed single long s in aſinalado is retained.
Completes diferente dos outros, different from others. It belongs to the illustration of jiyo, not a new headword.
Jiyoo denotes one's private need or business, explained by mizukara no yoo. Both long-o marks are circumflexes; the Portuguese noun continues on the next row.
De completes neceßidade. Jiyoo ga gozaru means having private business or a particular need; the whole Portuguese Ter belongs to italic type, not the OCR's split T/er.
Completes neceßidade particular, then gives jiyoo ni maitta, coming on private business. The scan reads maitta, not OCR moitta.

runs.text: a hum negocio, ou neceßidade particular.

lines.note: Completes vim: I came for a particular matter or need. The printed historical forms hum and neceßidade are retained.
Jiyuu is freedom. The example begins jiyuu jizai ni furumoo, behaving freely and at will; the headword's u carries a caron, not the OCR grave.
Moo completes the historically contracted furumoo across the line break. The Portuguese explains free, unconstrained conduct.
Jiyuuna is the adjectival form, free or unconstrained. The initial is I rather than OCR F; the example starts jiyuuna koto wo.

runs.text: Fazer as couſas à ſua vontade, &

lines.note: Suru completes the example, doing things at one's own will. The Portuguese continues with the manner adverb below.
Completes the explanation with freely. It is a continuation of the example, not the following adverbial headword.

The Portuguese defines the adverb 'freely'. The scan clearly prints Iixǔni with x, while the example on the same row has Iiyǔni with y. Retain the anomalous headword rather than silently substituting the lexical index's expected form.
Mono wo yuu completes the example, speaking freely. The scan has yǔ followed by a period, not the OCR's extra final i.

runs.text: expeditamẽte, ou cõ algũa liberdade, & ſoltura.

lines.note: Expands the speaking manner as readily, with freedom and lack of restraint. The abbreviated nasal vowels in expeditamẽte and cõ are retained.
Jizai means freedom or being at one's own disposal, with mizukara ari as the Japanese explanation. It is distinct from the physical implement in the next entry.

runs.text: Bambu de que pendurão o caldeirão de

lines.note: This jizai is a bamboo support from which a kettle hangs. The description identifies a hearth implement rather than the abstract freedom sense.
Completes the description: the hot-water kettle is suspended over the fire. It belongs wholly to the preceding implement entry.
Jizaiten is identified as the name of a heaven. The initial capital I, not OCR t, is supported by the neighbouring Iizai entries and the scan.

This begins the consonantal-I-before-O section and means a prologue, jo. The initial I is enlarged and was clipped by the supplied crop; the following rounded letter is read as an unaccented capital O, not supplied with the next entry's caron.
Joo is explained by kami, ue, noboru and agaru: above, the upper part, and upward movement. Cami, not OCR Camui, is visible; the whole Portuguese Em is italic.
Completes em cima and adds the upper part and rising. Item introduces another related sense on the next line.
Adds high or excellent, then introduces joogé as the paired notion of highs and lows. The gloss continues below.
Completes altos e baixos and adds the verbal sense of going up and down. Decer is the printed historical spelling.
Miyako e jooge wo itasu means going to and coming from the capital. The scan supports Miacoye rather than OCR Mincoye.
Completes the capital-travel example; Vide infrà directs the reader to a later entry. Miaco is the Portuguese form in this italic sentence, not a roman Japanese example.
This joo means a fortress, explicitly shiro. The example starts retiring within the fortress; the scan has a paragraph mark, without the OCR's extra period after it.
Completes hiki shirizoku across the physical break. The Portuguese describes retreating into the fortress and divides fortale-za.
Za completes fortaleza. Joo wo otosu is equated with semeotosu, taking a fortress by attack; Com begins combater, without a securely printed terminal hyphen.
Completes combater and adds bringing down the fortress. It is the translation of the preceding Japanese example.
This joo means a letter. The example says the addressee's letter has safely arrived; the printed initial I, missing from OCR, remains visible.

The Japanese epistolary ending completes the statement that the letter duly arrived, matching the Portuguese. Enlargement shows no secure circumflex over the first o, so the selected text is ſoro rather than the draft's ſôro. Voſſa has two long ſ letters.
